155.title: *you can do this*
155.hook: a calendar with five limbs, a moon that sets the dates, and nobody who keeps every festival
155.howItsDone: Hindu families usually keep the festivals their region, family and temple keep, finding the lunar dates each year in a panchang, a printed almanac or app, and marking them at home in small ways as well as large.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the second half of Pongal Onam: a flower carpet growing at the door for a king who comes home once a year. What did you get ready? Today, the whole year, and how to hold it. Day one hundred fifty-five.

In the last two and a half weeks you've been through a lot of festivals. Five days of Diwali. Holi's fire and colors. Nine nights of Navaratri. A midnight cradle. A clay Ganesha, welcomed and let go. A night awake for Shiva. A thread. Kites. A pot boiling over. A king coming home. If you're feeling a small wave of panic, that's fair. How is anyone supposed to keep all of that? Here's the honest answer, and it's a relief. Almost nobody does.
screen: `TEN FESTIVALS, TWO AND A HALF WEEKS.` → `HOW DOES ANYONE KEEP ALL THAT?` → `ALMOST NOBODY DOES.`

segments.voice: Start with how the year is counted. Most of these festivals are set by the moon. A Hindu month has a bright half, as the moon grows, and a dark half, as it shrinks, and each lunar day is called a tithi. Janmashtami is the eighth of the dark half. Ganesh Chaturthi is the fourth of the bright half. That's why the dates move around your wall calendar every year. Every so often an extra month is added, so the moon's year doesn't drift too far from the seasons. And there are a few solar days, like Makar Sankranti, that stay put. To find the dates, families use a panchang, an almanac. The word means five limbs: the lunar day, the weekday, the star the moon is passing, and two more ways of dividing time. Some families keep a printed one on the kitchen wall; now there are apps. Second thing: nobody keeps them all. A family in Kolkata lives for Durga Puja. A family in Pune lives for Ganesha. In Kerala it's Onam; in Tamil Nadu, Pongal. Families keep what their region, their parents and their temple keep, and add what they love. That isn't doing it wrong. That's how festivals are kept. Third: a festival doesn't need to be big to count. A lamp on Diwali. A pinch of color on Holi. Staying up one watch on Shivaratri. One thread. The tradition itself is full of small, real ways in. So here's what this whole camp has been saying, in one line. You don't have to do everything. You have to do something, on purpose, and do it again next year.
screen: `THE MOON SETS THE DATES.` · `A PANCHANG: THE FIVE LIMBS.` · `NOBODY KEEPS THEM ALL.` · `SMALL COUNTS.` · then, large: `SOMETHING, ON PURPOSE, AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose your three. Settle, and breathe. Let the festivals pass through your mind like floats in a parade. Diwali's lamps. Holi's colors. Navaratri's nine nights. The midnight cradle. Ganesha in clay. The Shivaratri vigil. The rakhi. Kites. The pot. The flower carpet. Don't decide yet. Just notice which ones made something in you lean forward. Now pick three. Only three. For each, picture the smallest real way you could keep it this year. One lamp. One watch. One thread. Hold your three. The bell holds the time.
You can do this. Not all of it. Something, on purpose, the next time the moon comes round.
Your line: you can do this. Today, look up when your first of the three falls this year, and put it in your calendar. Day one hundred fifty-five.

156.title: Camp 3 close
156.hook: assemble your practice — morning, sunset, weekly, yearly
156.howItsDone: Many Hindus keep a daily rhythm of a short morning puja or prayer and an evening lamp or arti, add weekly or twice-monthly observances like a temple visit or an Ekadashi fast, and keep the festivals their family and region observe through the year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, you can do this: the moon sets the dates, nobody keeps every festival, and you chose your three. Did one go in the calendar? Today, the last day of the practices. Day one hundred fifty-six.

Sixty days ago, this camp started with the breath you already have. Since then you've collected a lot of pieces. A few ways to breathe. A mantra. A shelf with five things on it. A flame circled at sunset. A way to walk into a temple. A year of festivals. Pieces are nice, but pieces in a drawer don't do much. Today we take them out and put them together, the way you'd set a table: something for the morning, something for sunset, something for the week, and something for the year. Then this camp closes, and we open a book.
screen: `SIXTY DAYS OF PIECES.` → `SET THE TABLE.` → `THEN WE OPEN A BOOK.`

segments.voice: Morning first. The breath week gave you prana, the breath as life, and a handful of ways to work with it: the pause called kumbhaka, alternate nostrils, nadi shodhana, the humming bee, bhramari, the ocean-sound ujjayi. Put two minutes of pranayama together. The mantra week gave you your ishta, the form that fits you, japa on a mala of 108, and ajapa, the mantra that says itself. The shrine week gave you deepa, the lamp, pushpa, the flower, ghanta, the bell, water, and naivedya, food offered and shared. That's a morning puja in four minutes. Sunset next. Sandhya, the junction of the day. A flame circled in arti, the light taken to your eyes, or just the real sun going down in the west. Then weekly. Surya namaskar, bowing to the sun with your body. A vrata, a vow, often a fast, taken on by choice. Ekadashi, twice a month, if you want a rhythm. And the mandir: darshan, seeing and being seen, walking the circle, singing with a room full of people. Then yearly: the festivals, and the three you picked. Here's the thing about all of it. Nobody does the whole list. A real practice is small enough to survive a bad Tuesday. Pick one morning thing, one sunset thing, one weekly thing, and your three festivals. That's a practice. And the tradition has a word for coming back to it again and again, a word Krishna uses in the Gita, coming soon: abhyasa. Practice, repeated. Tomorrow, the text. Camp four is the Bhagavad Gita, read in order, beginning with two armies on a field.
screen: `MORNING: BREATH, MANTRA, SHRINE.` · `SUNSET: THE FLAME, OR THE SUN.` · `WEEKLY: BODY, FAST, TEMPLE.` · `YEARLY: YOUR THREE FESTIVALS.` · then, large: `SMALL ENOUGH TO SURVIVE A TUESDAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: build it now. Settle, and breathe. Morning: pick one thing. A slow breath, one round of a mantra, one lamp. See yourself doing it tomorrow, before your phone. Sunset: pick one thing. A flame, or just facing the light as it goes. Weekly: pick one. A temple visit, a small fast, sun salutations on Sunday. Yearly: your three festivals. Now see all four together, like a table set for someone you love. It's yours. It fits. The bell holds the time.
Camp three, closed. Sixty days of practices, from the breath you already have to a year of festivals, put together into something that's yours.
Your line: camp three close. Today, write your four down: morning, sunset, weekly, yearly. Put the list where you'll see it tomorrow morning. Day one hundred fifty-six.

157.title: The armies; the conch shells (1.1–1.19)
157.hook: a blind king asks what happened on the field, and a man with borrowed sight begins to tell him
157.howItsDone: Many Hindus read or chant the Bhagavad Gita at home or in study groups, often a chapter at a time; the whole text is framed as Sanjaya's report to the blind king Dhritarashtra, and chapter one opens on the field of Kurukshetra.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Camp 3 close: morning, sunset, weekly, yearly, a practice small enough to survive a Tuesday. Is your list where you can see it? Today, a new camp, and a book. Day one hundred fifty-seven.

Welcome to camp four. For the next eleven weeks we read one book, in order: the Bhagavad Gita, the Song of the Lord. Eighteen chapters; tradition counts seven hundred verses. You met these people in the stories: the Pandava brothers, their cousins the Kauravas, Krishna taking the reins of Arjuna's chariot on the eve of war. The Gita begins right there. But the very first voice in it isn't Krishna's, and it isn't Arjuna's. It's an old blind king, far from the battle, asking a question. Here it is, in Edwin Arnold's translation from 1885: "Ranged thus for battle on the sacred plain— On Kurukshetra—say, Sanjaya! say What wrought my people, and the Pandavas?"
screen: `CAMP FOUR: ONE BOOK, IN ORDER.` → `A BLIND KING ASKS.` → then, large: `WHAT WROUGHT MY PEOPLE?`

segments.voice: The king is Dhritarashtra, father of the Kauravas. He can't see, and he isn't on the field. The sage Vyasa has given his minister, Sanjaya, the sight to see the whole battle from the palace. So the entire Gita is a report, told to a blind father who already fears the answer. In Sanskrit his first words are: Dharmakshetre kurukshetre samaveta yuyutsavah. On the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus, gathered, eager to fight. Notice he calls it two things at once. A real place, Kurukshetra, north of Delhi, where pilgrims still go. And dharmakshetra, the field of dharma, of what's right. Sanjaya begins. Duryodhana, the eldest Kaurava, walks up to his old teacher Drona and starts listing warriors, ours and theirs, a little too fast, like someone nervous talking over the silence. Then old Bhishma, the great-uncle, to cheer him, roars like a lion and blows his conch shell. And the whole field answers: conches, drums, horns, all at once. On the other side, in a great chariot yoked to white horses, Krishna and Arjuna blow their conches. Krishna's is called Panchajanya. Arjuna's, Devadatta. Bhima's, the giant one, Paundra. Every brother has his own. And the sound, Sanjaya says, tears at the hearts of the Kauravas and echoes through earth and sky. Here's why this opening matters. Many readers, Gandhi among them, have heard the field as more than a place: the field is a human life, where the right and the easy line up and face each other. Either way, the book starts where your hard days start. Everyone's in position. The noise is deafening. Nobody has moved yet.
screen: `A REPORT TO A BLIND FATHER.` · `THE FIELD OF DHARMA.` · `A LIST TOO FAST, THEN THE CONCHES.` · `THE FIELD IS A LIFE, TOO.` · then, large: `EVERYONE'S IN POSITION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand on your field. Settle, and breathe. Picture a wide plain at dawn. On it, lined up, the things you're facing right now. A decision. A person. A deadline. A fear. Let them take their places. Now let the noise come: the conches, the drums, all the voices in your head blowing at once. Don't fight it. Just hear it. Then, underneath the noise, notice your breath, still going, steady, like Sanjaya quietly telling what he sees. Nobody has to move yet. Just stand on the field and look. The bell holds the time.
The armies. Two sides of one family, lined up on Kurukshetra, the field of dharma, and a roar of conch shells before anyone moves.
Your line: the field. Today, when your day gets loud, name the field you're standing on, and take one breath before you move. Day one hundred fifty-seven.

158.title: Arjuna asks to see (1.20–1.27)
158.hook: the greatest archer asks for his chariot between the armies, to get a good look at the enemy, and Krishna parks it in front of his grandfather
158.tomorrow: "I see no good in killing my kin" (1.28–1.39)
158.howItsDone: Readers of the Gita often pause on 1.21–1.27, where Krishna drives Arjuna's chariot between the armies and stops before Bhishma and Drona; some readers hear Krishna's first words, telling Arjuna to look, as the quiet start of all that follows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the armies: a blind king asking, conch shells roaring, and your line was the field. What field did you stand on? Today, Arjuna asks for one thing, and gets it. Day one hundred fifty-eight.

The conches have finished roaring. Arrows are about to fly. And Arjuna, the archer, lifts his bow. Over his chariot flies his banner, and on it is Hanuman, the monkey who carried a mountain, the one you met on this path. Arjuna turns to his driver, Krishna, and asks for something that sounds perfectly sensible. He wants a look. Drive me out between the two armies, he says, so I can see who I'm fighting. It's what any good commander would do. Check the other side. Size them up. Krishna says nothing. He just drives.
screen: `HANUMAN ON THE BANNER.` → `DRIVE ME OUT BETWEEN THEM.` → `KRISHNA JUST DRIVES.`

segments.voice: In Sanskrit, Arjuna's request is: senayor ubhayor madhye ratham sthapaya me 'chyuta. Between both armies, set my chariot, Achyuta, unfailing one. He wants to see, he says, those who've come to fight for Duryodhana. He's thinking of enemies. Now watch where Krishna stops. Sanjaya tells the king: Krishna drove the chariot between the armies, and set it down right in front of Bhishma and Drona. Bhishma, the great-uncle Arjuna grew up calling grandfather. Drona, the teacher who taught him to shoot. Of all the places on that huge field, Krishna parks there. And he says just one line, his first words in the whole Gita: Partha, look at these Kurus, gathered together. Look at them. Arjuna looks. And the text slows down and lists what he sees, one by one: fathers, grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, friends, fathers-in-law. Every one of them is family, or nearly. He asked to see the enemy, and he saw his people. The verse says he was overcome with pity, and he began to speak, in sorrow. Notice what Krishna doesn't do. He doesn't argue, doesn't warn, doesn't explain. He doesn't say, are you sure? He just puts Arjuna exactly where he'll have to see the truth, and lets him look. A fight looks easy from a distance. The other side is a category: them. Drive out into the middle, stop in front of real faces, and the category falls apart. Everything the Gita says next starts from this moment. A man who asked to see, and saw too much.
screen: `SET MY CHARIOT BETWEEN THE ARMIES.` · `KRISHNA STOPS BEFORE BHISHMA, DRONA.` · `PARTHA, LOOK AT THEM.` · `HE ASKED FOR ENEMIES, SAW FAMILY.` · then, large: `LOOK AT THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drive out into the middle. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who's on the other side of something with you. At work, at home, in the news. Right now they're probably a category in your mind: them. Now picture Krishna driving your chariot out and stopping right in front of them. Look at their face. Who raised them? Who are they a father, a sister, a grandchild to? What did they look like at ten? You don't have to agree with them. Just look, and let them be a person for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Arjuna asks to see. He asks for his chariot between the armies, and Krishna stops it in front of the people he loves.
Your line: look at them. Today, when someone becomes a them in your head, stop, and picture their face up close. Day one hundred fifty-eight.

159.title: "I see no good in killing my kin" (1.28–1.39)
159.word: "I see no good in killing my kin"
159.hook: his legs give way, his mouth goes dry, the bow slips, and the greatest warrior alive makes his case against the war
159.howItsDone: Commentators on the Gita treat Arjuna's objection in 1.28–1.39 as a serious moral argument, and many readers see in it their own moments of doubt before a hard duty; the rest of the Gita is Krishna's answer to it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Arjuna asked to see, and Krishna stopped the chariot before his grandfather and his teacher. Your line was look at them. Whose face did you look at? Today, what Arjuna says when he's done looking. Day one hundred fifty-nine.

Think about the last time your body knew before you did. A phone call you didn't want to make, and your hands went cold. A room you didn't want to walk into, and your stomach turned. Arjuna has just looked at his whole family lined up to fight him. And before he can make a single argument, his body starts making it for him. His legs give way. His mouth dries up. He's shaking. The hair on his arms stands up. His skin burns. And Gandiva, the famous bow, starts slipping out of his hand. He can't stand. Then the words come.
screen: `THE BODY KNOWS FIRST.` → `LEGS GIVE WAY, MOUTH GOES DRY.` → `THE BOW SLIPS.`

segments.voice: Chapter one, verses twenty-eight to thirty-nine, is Arjuna's objection, and it's worth hearing on its own terms, because the Gita takes it seriously. Is it cowardice? Many readers hear conscience. In Sanskrit, the heart of it: na cha shreyo 'nupashyami hatva svajanam ahave. And I see no good in killing my own people in battle. Then he goes further. Na kankshe vijayam Krishna, na cha rajyam sukhani cha. I don't want victory, Krishna, or a kingdom, or pleasures. What would a kingdom even be for, he asks, if the people we wanted it for are the ones lying dead on this field? Teachers, fathers, sons, grandfathers, uncles. Even if they kill me, he says, I don't want to kill them. Not for all three worlds, let alone for this earth. And then his sharpest point. Yes, the Kauravas are in the wrong. Their minds are clouded by greed; they can't see the evil of destroying a family. But we can see it, he says. Why shouldn't we, who see clearly, turn back? That's a real argument. People have made it at every war since. And here's what's striking about the Gita: it gives Arjuna twelve verses to make his case, fully, in his own words, before anyone answers. Krishna doesn't interrupt. When he does answer, in the next chapter, his first words are blunt: he calls this a weakness of the heart. Commentators have argued ever since over whether Arjuna's case is conscience or confusion. But the reply, which takes the rest of the book, is a reply to this, the honest objection, heard in full. A good teacher lets you say the whole thing.
screen: `COWARDICE, OR CONSCIENCE?` · `I SEE NO GOOD IN KILLING MY KIN.` · `NO KINGDOM IS WORTH THEM.` · `THEY CAN'T SEE. WE CAN. TURN BACK.` · then, large: `HEARD IN FULL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let your objection speak. Settle, and breathe. Think of something in front of you that part of you really doesn't want to do. First, just notice the body: where does it tighten, where does it go cold? Let that be there. Then let the objection talk, fully, in its own words, the way Arjuna does. Don't answer it yet. Don't argue. Don't shame it. Just listen, all the way to the end, like a good teacher would. You might be surprised what it says. The bell holds the time.
I see no good in killing my kin. Arjuna's case against the war: no victory, no kingdom, is worth the people he loves.

segments.voice: Your line: the honest objection. Today, when someone pushes back, let them finish, the whole thing, before you answer. Day one hundred fifty-nine.

160.title: The bow drops (1.40–1.47)
160.hook: the last argument, the last verse of chapter one, and a warrior sitting down in the middle of the field
160.howItsDone: Chapter one of the Gita is traditionally titled Arjuna Vishada Yoga, the yoga of Arjuna's despair; many readers and teachers treat Arjuna's collapse at 1.47 as the necessary starting point for the teaching that follows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, I see no good in killing my kin: Arjuna's case against the war, heard in full. Your line was the honest objection. Did you let someone finish? Today, the end of chapter one. Day one hundred sixty.

Some people know this moment. Weeks of holding it together. Every argument made, to themselves and to everyone else. And then, one ordinary afternoon, in a parking lot or a kitchen or an office bathroom, they just sit down. Not because they decided to. Because they can't stand up anymore. That's where chapter one of the Gita ends. Not with a battle. With the warrior Krishna drove into the middle of the field sitting down in his chariot, and his bow on the floor.
screen: `WEEKS OF HOLDING IT TOGETHER.` → `ONE AFTERNOON, THEY SIT DOWN.` → `THE BOW ON THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Arjuna's last arguments, in verses forty to forty-four, are about what a war like this destroys beyond the dead. When a family is wiped out, he says, its old ways die with it: the rites, the offerings to the ancestors, the order that held a society together. Chaos follows, and the generations after are lost. It's the argument of a man from his own time and world, and people read it differently today; some commentators hear in it a real grief for everything a war erases, and some hear a mind grabbing any argument it can find. Either way, it ends in a cry. Alas, he says, we're about to commit a great wrong, killing our own people out of greed for a kingdom. Then the line that's hardest to hear. It would be better for me, he says, if the sons of Dhritarashtra, weapons in hand, killed me in battle, unarmed and not fighting back. And then Sanjaya, telling the blind king, describes what he sees. In Sanskrit: visrijya sasharam chapam shoka samvigna manasah. Casting aside his bow and arrows, his mind shaken with grief. Arjuna sinks down onto the seat of his chariot, there between the two armies. That's the end of chapter one. And here's the surprise. Every chapter of the Gita has a title calling it a yoga, a path. This one is called Arjuna Vishada Yoga. The yoga of Arjuna's despair. Despair, counted as a path. Nothing that follows, none of Krishna's teaching, happens without this. The book begins because a man sat down and said, I can't.
screen: `WHAT A WAR ERASES.` · `BETTER IF THEY KILLED ME UNARMED.` · `HE CASTS ASIDE HIS BOW.` · `THE YOGA OF DESPAIR.` · then, large: `THE BOOK BEGINS WITH I CAN'T.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: put the bow down. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you've been carrying and fighting with for too long. Picture it as a bow, heavy in your hands, arrows on your back. Now, without making any decision about tomorrow, just set it down beside you. Let your hands be empty. Sit down, the way Arjuna sits in his chariot, right in the middle of everything. You don't have to fix anything yet. Saying I can't, honestly, is the start of the book. The bell holds the time.
The bow drops. The last verse of chapter one: Arjuna casts aside his bow and arrows and sits down, his mind shaken with grief.

161.title: Krishna's first words: "whence this dejection?" (2.1–2.10)
161.hook: Krishna's answer to a man in tears is not comfort; it's a jolt, and then Arjuna asks to be taught
161.tomorrow: The self that is not slain (2.11–2.25)
161.howItsDone: Commentators often treat Gita 2.7, where Arjuna says he is Krishna's student and asks to be taught, as the moment the teaching truly begins, and 2.3's call to cast off faintness and stand up is often quoted in times of discouragement.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bow drops: Arjuna sat down in his chariot, and chapter one ended. Your line was I can't. Did you say it to someone? Today, Krishna answers. And a look back at the week. Day one hundred sixty-one.

Here's what kindness usually sounds like. A friend is sitting on the floor in tears, saying I can't do this, and someone kneels down, puts a hand on their back, and says: it's okay, you don't have to. Now here's Krishna, with his friend in exactly that state, in the middle of a battlefield. And the first thing he says is closer to: what is this? Where did this come from? Get up. Chapter two begins, and it begins with a jolt.
screen: `A FRIEND ON THE FLOOR, IN TEARS.` → `IT'S OKAY, YOU DON'T HAVE TO.` → `KRISHNA SAYS: GET UP.`

segments.voice: Sanjaya sets the scene: Arjuna, overcome with pity, eyes full of tears. He's already had one line from Krishna, look at them. Now come Krishna's first words of real answer. In Sanskrit: kutas tva kashmalam idam vishame samupasthitam. Older English translators rendered it something like, whence this dejection, at this hour of crisis? Where has this come from, now of all times? Then: klaibyam ma sma gamah Partha. Don't give in to this unmanly weakness. And: tyaktvottishtha parantapa. Cast off this petty faintness of heart and stand up, you who scorch your foes. Stand up. It sounds harsh. But notice what Krishna is doing. He's not agreeing with the story Arjuna is telling about himself. He's reminding him who he is. And it doesn't work, not yet. Arjuna argues again. How can I shoot arrows at Bhishma and Drona, who deserve my worship? Better to live as a beggar. I don't even know which is better, winning or losing. And then he says the sentence that turns the whole book: shishyas te 'ham shadhi mam tvam prapannam. I am your student. Teach me. I've come to you for refuge. After that, he says, I will not fight, and he falls silent. And Krishna, between the two armies, answers him, the text says, as if smiling. The jolt wasn't the teaching. The jolt got Arjuna to ask. And that's the week: a camp closed, a book opened, two armies, a request to see, an honest objection, a bow on the floor, and now a student, asking.
screen: `WHENCE THIS DEJECTION?` · `CAST IT OFF AND STAND UP.` · `I AM YOUR STUDENT. TEACH ME.` · `HE ANSWERS, AS IF SMILING.` · then, large: `STAND UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: from sitting down to asking. Settle, and breathe. Go back to the bow you set down yesterday, the thing that's too much. You don't have to pick it up. But try a different sentence. Instead of I can't, try: teach me. Say it inside, to God if you pray, or to life, or to your own wiser self. Teach me how to face this. Then just listen, and breathe, and notice what changes in your body when you move from giving up to asking. Imagine someone answering, as if smiling. The bell holds the time.
Krishna's first words. Where has this faintness come from, at this hour? Cast it off, and stand up.
Your line: stand up. Today, when you catch yourself sinking, stand up, literally, and ask one person to teach you something. Day one hundred sixty-one.
